Exchange rate forecasts for selected currencies 177 CRU International Limited confidential Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q1 # Executive summary #### Palladium: large deficits become the new market reality Having moved into deficit in 2010 for the first time in seven years, the palladium market was brought back into large surplus in 2011, even though, at the fundamental level, fabrication demand was still higher than mine and scrap supply. Unlike in 2010, the fundamental drivers were largely ignored by market players as both wild cards inherent to the palladium market – investmen

t demand and Russian state sales – came back into play. 



- In the next five years, we do not foresee any technological developments which could jeopardise the dominant role of the internal combustion engine and therefore threaten demand for palladium in catalytic converters. 



- Automakers in China, Japan and North America will continue consuming palladium in ever increasing volumes, providing strong price support.  Although demand from Europe is expected to stumble this year, this too will resuming an upward trajectory in 2013. 



- Demand from the electronics industry is expected to continue growing until the end of our forecast horizon, supported by growth in production of multi-layer ceramic capacitors.  The chemicals industry will also contribute to the growth in demand, although we do not expect this to kick in before 2015. 



- Overall, total palladium demand is forecast to grow in each of the next five years, at a compound annual rate of 6%. 



- Palladium mine production is set to grow at a compound annual rate of only 1.3% between 2012 and 2016.  Within this period, output is expected to contract in 2012 and 2013 before growth resumes in 2014.  Rising mining costs, falling grades, mine safety issues, strikes and other industrial actions will be the major limiting factors. 



- Russian state stocks of palladium are expected to become less important in terms of the palladium supply-demand balance in the years ahead. 



- As witnessed last year, strong fundamentals do not always guarantee strong price performance.  Therefore, investment demand will be vital in determining the future direction of the price. 



- We expect that palladium’s bull run will continue over the next five years with the real price averaging $987/oz over the period.

#### Other precious metal markets 

###### Gold 

Gold’s market surplus is likely to expand over the next two years, driven by weakening fabrication demand and growing mine supply.  However, after peaking in 2013, the surplus may then decline during the 2014-16 period, driven by slowing mine production, tighter scrap supplies and stronger demand for jewellery caused by lower prices and rising incomes. 



- Investor interest is stabilising while central bank buying continues to provide support, but greater market stresses are now needed to drive each fresh wave of buying interest. 



- Imposition of higher import duty on gold imports in India will reduce local and global demand for gold and may cost the country its title of the largest gold jewellery consumer. 

###### Silver 

After suffering more than gold in 2011 Q4, with the gold:silver price ratio rising from 53 to 59 in December, silver began to benefit from its industrial metal credentials early in 2012 as nervousness about the global economy has let up a little.  However, investor demand will still drive future prices. 



- Despite a

slight improvement in sentiment towards the economy in recent months, we have cut our projections of economic activity in each of the next five years.  This has reduced our estimate of total offtake in 2016 by 275 tonnes so that demand now grows to 29,450 tonnes. 



- Although projects have been proceeding, finance is hard to come by on terms that are 

- acceptable to potential producers.  We believe that this, as well as lower prices, will help to hold Western output back behind its full potential in 2016 by about 2,000 tonnes. 



- With interest rates unlikely to begin rising notably in 2014, we do expect silver’s price to fall before then.  Even then, we believe that the market will be running a surplus of about 4,000 t/y. 

###### Platinum 

Unlike in our December forecast, we now foresee the platinum market shifting into fundamental deficit in 2014. 



- Taking into account the strong likelihood of a return to recession this year for many European countries, demand for platinum in this key region is likely to decline before it starts growing again. 



- The supply of platinum remains constrained.  The sharp decline in the platinum price from mid- to late 2011 prompted some South African platinum miners to cut production and reduce their capital expenditure. 



- Since last September platinum has been trading largely at a discount to gold due to the grim outlook for the global economy and industrial demand.

# Chapter 1 Palladium 

#### 1.  Summary 

Over the next five years, the palladium market is set to move into a very large fundamental deficit owing to robust demand and lagging supply. 

The automotive sector should continue to be a source of strength for palladium demand over the next several years as carmakers continue to expand and build new production facilities in North America, China and other emerging markets.  In addition, further increases in palladium loadings due to tightening emissions standards and ongoing substitution of more expensive platinum in diesel passenger car catalysts should amplify demand for this metal. 

Meanwhile, mine and scrap supply will fail to match palladium fabrication demand in any of the next five years as growth prospects for the supply of palladium are quiet limited.  In fact, we do not envision any growth in 2012 and 2013 because we expect mine output to be even lower than last year in both Russia and South Africa and anticipate a sharp deceleration of production growth in North America.  Although supplies from secondary sources are expected to gr

ow at the same pace as palladium demand, this will be from a much lower base and thus would only cushion some of the weakness in mine production; it will not entirely offset it. As such, the gap between demand and supply is poised to widen in the years ahead and this means that other sources, like Russian state reserves or investor holdings, will have to be net suppliers to fill the growing void in the physical market. However, palladium deliveries from Russia are gradually losing their influence on the market as stocks decline and exports from Russia slow both to Switzerland and to centres of fabrication. As such, the metal held in ETFs and elsewhere will be in demand to help fill the gap left by lagging supply. And investors are unlikely to release the metal they hold unless they receive ever increasing prices. One large caveat to our forecast would be if the European financial situation deteriorates further. In that case commodity prices, including that of palladium, may be expected to slip again on a probable easing in global economic growth. Assuming the worst scenario does not materialise, we forecast an average real price of around $780/oz in 2012 and $900/oz in 2013. In our view, tightening physical market fundamentals from 2014 should eventually push the price above the $1,000/oz mark. Indeed, as the market deficit continues to widen, we expect the real price to average $1,150/oz in the final year of our forecast. ational|1,080|1,150| ###### **Note on sources and definitions** Although many of the statistics used in this analysis are taken from _Johnson Matthey_ , there are some important differences between the ways in which we each use these to explain market events. On the **demand** side, _Johnson Matthey’s_ figures generally show net consumption in each end-use, that is the difference between purchases and the amount of metal recovered from old scrap. In contrast, we prefer to list demand gross, and treat the metal recovered from the recycling of end-of-life products as an additional element of supply. In terms of the historical balance, this of course has no effect, since our higher gross consumption is offset one-for-one by higher secondary supply. However, because (a) we feel that economic and other developments drive demand at the gross level and (b) we feel that scrap recovery is driven mainly by consumption in some prior period, this different approach does yield different results when projecting net metal use forward. On the **supply** side, whilst _Johnson Matthey_ generally defines primary output as metal sales by platinum producers, we have meanwhile built our series on the basis of recoverable output mine-by-mine. Through time, these two should of course be the same. And _Johnson Matthey’s_ approach is arguably better for assessing the historical balance year-by-year. However, our choice is again driven by considerations of the future, it being far easier to forecast production on a mine-by-mine basis than at the level of smelters’ and refineries’ metal sales. Finally, when looking at the **supply-demand balance** , we refuse to treat bar hoarding or ETFs as part of consumption. Instead, we see these as just another way in which investors hold excess stock, there being no difference between this identifiable material and the other inventories that are implied by the past imbalance between supply and demand. Stockholders will not maintain or build their positions unless they feel that this offers them some economic benefit. And this is just as true of “investors” as it is of any other market participant. Bars and ETFs may be a little less liquid than other surplus metal but, if stockholders’ mood changes, all previously accumulated metal will be a potential source of additional supply. Gross fabrication demand ###### 2.1 Summary We estimate that fabrication demand for palladium continued to recover last year and grew by nearly 4% to just over 10 Moz. This recovery was largely driven by the record volumes of palladium (5.9 Moz) used to equip the exhaus

t catalytic convertors of a record number of vehicles produced globally. Vehicle production was strong in all major regions apart from Japan where output was negatively affected by disruption caused by the March earthquake and tsunami and Thai floods in the latter part of the year. Demand from the chemical and electrical/electronics sectors was also robust in 2011. Consumption of palladium by the global chemical industry continued to rise driven by significant capacity expansion in the downstream polyester industry in the key markets of China and India. As a result, gross demand for palladium from this sector increased by 6.4% year-onyear and reached a new record of 1,575 koz. As for the electrical/electronics sector, demand for palladium went up by 5.3% to 1,485 koz on the back of the continuous increase in the number of multi-layered capacitors required for high-specification electronic devices. Demand from the dental sector remained essentially unchanged at 595 koz, while net metal purchases for jewellery manufacture slumped by 32% from 495 koz in 2010 to just 335 koz in 2011. Rising palladium prices discouraged consumers from buying palladium jewellery and encouraged the industry to recycle and remanufacture old stock, which led to cannibalisation of new palladium demand. ###### **North America** 

Palladium consumption by the North American automotive sector peaked in 2000 at 2.7 Moz boosted by the record number of vehicles produced in the region during that year.  Demand has largely been on the downtrend since then as falling vehicle output prompted car manufacturers to adjust their metal needs.  When the recent economic crisis reached its trough in 2009, metal consumption collapsed to just above 1 Moz.  Only that much of palladium was required to equip exhaust catalytic convertors of 8.7 million vehicles produced in that year, the lowest output since 1981. 

In 2010, however, the trend in palladium demand reversed as regional vehicle output rebounded by 38% to over 12 million units amid strengthening consumer confidence in the USA.  As a result, palladium consumption also so

ared but at a slightly slower pace; demand increased by 33% to 1,355 koz.  The difference between the two growth rates was explained by the fact that, against the backdrop of rising fuel prices, consumer preferences began to shift towards smaller cars equipped with smaller petrol engines which in turn have lower palladium loadings.  Therefore, the increase in regional vehicle manufacturing was not fully matched by an increase in demand for palladium due to an increased percentage of small cars on US roads. 

In 2011, vehicle assemblies continued to recover from the dramatic downturn in 2009 and approximated 13.4 million units, a gain of about 10% on the previous year.  As in 2010, the improvement in vehicle output was largely driven by the ongoing strong recovery in the USA, aided by consumers’ need to replace aging vehicles, which many had delayed during the late2000s recession.  As purchases were deferred, the average age of vehicles on the country’s roads had increased to a record 10.8 years (up from 9.8 years in 2007). 

Unlike in 2010, last year’s growth in vehicle manufacturing was closely matched by a nearly symmetric increase in palladium demand.  Indeed, after showing slower than expected growth in the first half of 2011, the US economy rebounded strongly in the second half of the year and boosted demand for larger vehicles, whose emissions systems are loaded with more metal.  For instance, last year’s production of heavy commercial vehicles soared by 53% year-on-year to reach 430,000 units, its highest level since the onset of the global economic crisis.  Given that the region is primarily a petrol market, palladium was the main beneficiary from these developments.  As a result, gross demand for the metal increased by 9% from 1,355 koz in 2010 to 1,480 koz in 2011.  Even so, metal consumption has not yet fully recovered to its pre-recession level and was still 13% below nearly 1,700 koz consumed in 2007. Continued impressive growth in US car sales has been attributed to further replacement demand, decreasing unemployment and gains in consumer confidence that the economy may finally be heading for a solid recovery. According to the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA), in 2011, Japanese vehicle sales and production dropped by 15% and 11.5% respectively from a year earlier, owing to the decline in buying interest and production of new cars following the effects of the triple disaster that occurred last March and Thai flooding in the second half of last year. ###### 2.5  Jewellery fabrication 

###### **Historical developments** 

Palladium was first used for jewellery during World War II when platinum was declared a strategic metal and reserved for military use.  Once wartime restrictions had been lifted, however, jewellers wanting white metal returned to using platinum or white gold because palladium was much harder to work after casting.  Even today, the lion’s share of palladium consumption is accounted for

by industrial applications: autocatalysts (59%), chemical manufacture (16%), electronics (15%) and dentistry (6%) account for a combined 96%.  Out of the remaining 4%, jewellery’s share is only 3%, which means that, among the main four precious metals, this component of demand is the smallest for palladium.  By comparison, jewellery accounted for 18% of platinum fabrication demand last year, and 71% of fabrication demand for gold<sup>*</sup> .

Hardly surprisingly, both physically and chemically, palladium bears a remarkable resemblance to platinum.  Like platinum, palladium is very hard and has the lustrous silverwhite colour that makes ornaments made of these metals so attractive. 

As with other precious metals, palladium is rarely used in its purest form by jewellers, but instead is normally alloyed with lesser metals in order to achieve the desired strength and durability.  Palladium alloys typically contain 95% palladium and about 5% ruthenium.  The metal is used both in such alloys and as a substitute for nickel when making white gold. Palladium-gold is a much more expensive alloy than nickel-gold but is hypoallergenic and holds its white colour better.  The metal is also used in watchmaking. 

Despite the abovementioned similarities with platinum, palladium has never caught on in terms of popularity and recognition to the same extent as its sister metal.  In fact, there are some significant differences between these two metals, which pose both advantages and disadvantages for the use of palladium in jewellery manufacture. 

On the positive side, palladium has a density of 12 g/cm<sup>3</sup> while that of platinum is almost double at 21 g/cm<sup>3</sup> , and this offers the potential for significant savings when it comes to purchasing palladium jewellery.  Jewellery is priced not only according to the labour that is involved in its manufacture (particularly in the case of hand-made jewellery) but also according to the weight of the metal used.  Therefore, when compared with an identically designed platinum ring, a palladium ring will weigh significantly less and will thus cost less even at identical prices.  The low density is also an advantage in items where lower weight is important, such earrings and necklaces as well as chunky dress rings and bangles. 

On the flip side, palladium is still poorly recognised and accepted by jewellery consumers. While palladium heads for stone settings have been available for many years, the availability of finished jewellery made of palladium is still quite new.  In addition, for a long time, many jewellers found palladium d

ifficult to work due to the severe porosity produced during the casting of traditional 95:5 palladium-ruthenium alloys. 

It was in fact only in the early 2000s, when gold and platinum prices began to rise steeply, that palladium began to make serious inroads into the jewellery industry.  And jewellers’ net demand for the metal has been predominantly on a downward trend since 2005 due to waning interest from China, the major consumer of palladium jewellery, and rising prices.  In 2011, the palladium jewellery market continued to shrink as elevated prices reduced affordability for consumers and encouraged retailers to recycle unsold palladium pieces simply to crystallise the profit made on the metal price.  As a result, recycling rates increased and manufacturing output continued to soften with net demand for new palladium from this source slumping by 32% at the global level from 495 koz in 2010 to just 335 koz in 2011. 

###### **China** 

China dominates palladium jewellery demand.  The popularity of palladium jewellery took off in China in the early 2000s, once platinum prices rose to a level that choked off its own consumption.  Chinese jewellers were particularly interested in seeking a more affordable white metal, as many Asians feel that white jewellery has a more pleasing contrast with the Asian skin colour than other metals.  Of course, there was also white gold, but consumers in this region prefer a pure metal rather than a blend of several metals.  Palladium became more favoured and,

###### 3.1  Summary 

Substantial amounts of palladium are recycled each year and, although much of this never reaches the open market, we still think it should be counted as part of supply.  Even where recycled metal is moving in a closed circuit between manufacturer, end-user and refiner, scrap returns do not necessarily equate to new purchases one-for-one (if they did, there would be no net demand).  In addition, the palladium dispersed in spent autocatalysts and in old electronic circuits finds its way via the normal scrap network back to precious metals refiners. 

Most areas of the secondary palladium network reached maturity many years ago, with a high proportion of all available arisings already being recovered.  Future tonnage recycling in these areas will thus continue to be driven just by consumption at various points in the past. And, so long as there were no step changes in the historical demand trend, future recycling will continue along what are now well-established paths. 

These well-established paths have meant that secondary supply is perhaps the only component of the palladium supply-demand equation which has been expanding steadily since 1990 when our records begin.  The only year when it failed to increase was 2009 when a significant drop in the palladium price prompted some businesses and individual consumers to hold back metal in anticipation of prices going back up later.  Even then, the drop in recycling volumes was fairly moderate – 3.4% year-on-year or 85 koz.  And this loss was more than compensated in 2010 primarily due to the surge in recycling of autocatalysts (+36% year-on-year) sparked by the introduction of various government-backed scrappage schemes across the globe.

Moreover, it is estimated that approximately 400,000 cars were damaged beyond repair by last year’s tsunami, and we would expect the majority of these vehicles to be recycled at some point this year, adding to the amount of metal recovered in Japan. Similar cyclical swings have been witnessed in North America, albeit this time around a generally rising trend. The natural disaster in Japan, which dramatically reduced availability of many models for sale in the US car market, together with consumers’ hesitation to replace aging automobiles because of a high level of economic uncertainty, stoked demand for second-hand vehicles in the first half of 2011, meaning there were fewer vehicles, and by extension autocatalysts, available for recycling. However, the gradual improvement in the domestic economy towards the end of last year pushed new car purchases higher. As a result, secondhand ve

hicle prices stopped rising there and began to fall, suggesting that scrappage rates and palladium recovery improved.  As such, we estimate that a record 15 million US cars ended up in the country’s scrap yards last year.  This is 6% more than our estimate for 2010.  If consumer confidence continues to improve in the USA, we will see higher sales of new vehicles, which should translate into rising scrap rates and more palladium being recovered as a result. 

Recovery of palladium from autocatalysts in Europe is likely to have increased last year as the number of vehicles scrapped grew by around 20% to over 9 million cars.  Volumes of palladium recovered were boosted by higher sales in the first half of 2011, as well as higher palladium-loaded catalysts entering the recycling stream. 

By 2016, we expect the West European total to be up by almost another 5 million.  The number of Japanese vehicles being scrapped (these are all fitted with catalysts) may in contrast start to slide again after strong rises in 2012 and 2013.  And the number of scrapped vehicles of North American origin may follow a similar pattern.  However, some vehicles that were built with catalysts outside the OECD will begin to be scrapped too, so the total growth in the pool of potentially available units could be more than 25%. 

In the not-too-distant future, Asia will become a significant source of recyclable autocatalysts.  The developing Asian markets, such as China and India, as well as Russia, have been sharply increasing domestic auto production in recent years.  Since the vehicles sold in these markets are predominantly petrol-fuelled, palladium is the main metal used to clean their emissions.  As these countries gradually shift towards stricter new emission legislation, palladium loadings in their cars should therefore increase.  As such, we expect recovery in palladium from this source to get a significant boost in a few years time when these autocatalysts begin entering the recycling stream.

#### 4.  Mine production 

###### 4.1  Summary 

The recovery in palladium mine production, which had begun in 2010 after three years of continuous decline, continued in 2011.  Mine production rose to a total of 6,869 koz last year, up 3.7% or 247 koz from 2010.  The main contributor to the increase was a sharp growth in North America where combined production from the USA and Canada soared by 37.5% or 269 koz.  In addition, a strong performance by the Zimbabwean palladium miners, who increased output by 19% or 42 koz, also contributed to the last year’s growth.  The recovery, however, was not universal.  In contrast to 2010, Russia and South Africa, the two largest palladium producing countries, and Botswana reported a combined loss of 65 koz in 2011.  As a result, the pace of last year’s growth in global palladium production slowed in both absolute and relative terms compared with 2010, when the rises were 4.0% and 255 koz. 

A 2011 mine output of 6,869 koz is 59 koz, or 0.9%, higher than we expected when writing our last full palladium forecast 12 months ago.  However, in the light of recent production reports and company guidance, we have lowered our projection for 2012 to 6,791 koz from the 6,953 koz that we were fore

casting last March. The main reasons for this downgrade are an expectation of even lower than last year’s output in both Russia and South Africa coupled with a sharp deceleration of production growth in North America after the one-off surge in 2011 following the restart of Vale’s Sudbury operations in Canada. Prospects for palladium production in Zimbabwe, a potentially very promising supplier, are also clouded with political uncertainty which, together with regular increases in taxes and royalties, will continue to make Zimbabwe a difficult country in which to operate. We are therefore cautious about the growth potential of palladium mining there. We in fact now expect palladium mine output to contract by 1.1% in 2012 and shave an additional 0.3% in 2013 before growth resumes in 2014. In addition, we believe that there may be more room on the downside during the first two years of our outlook because any closure or mothballing of platinum mines due to low prices will have a negative impact on palladium output. By 2016, based on committed developments alone, and after allowing for normal disruptions to published plans, we expect global mine production to have risen by 6.6% from our estimated total of 6,869 koz for 2011. On an annual basis, we expect palladium production to grow at a compound annual rate of 1.3% over the next five years although, as we have already said, the actually pattern is expected to be down before turning more strongly up. Actual changes in production will therefore fluctuate between -1.1% in 2012 and +3.2% in 2014. Mines which have yet to start up or have only recently done so are projected to supply a cumulative 720 koz throughout the forecast period, or less than 2% of total 2012-16 output. Even by 2016, these may collectively be supplying only 225 koz/y before disruption, or just 2.9% of undisrupted supply. Depletions and exhaustions will be even less and cost the market only 24 koz/y between 2011 and 2016, so changes at other existing mines will be the main driver of aggregate production swings. Net expansions will add almost 800 koz/y to 2016 output before disruption, even though production at 25 mines will stay essentially unchanged. ###### **South Africa** 

All South African palladium production is derived as a by-product of platinum production. As a result, local palladium production is exposed to the same problems which face platinum miners.  Therefore, it is no surprise that South African palladium output declined last year following the drop in platinum production.  However, due to the fact that the scale of palladium production in the country is smaller than that of platinum, the losses incurred were also smaller; at 2,639 koz the metal’s production was just 1% below the 2010 level and just half the size of the annual loss attributed to platinum miners. 

The challenges facing the nation’s PGM producers are well known, and we have covered them extensively in our previous reports.  2011 was no different, with further frequent safety stoppages, strikes and industrial actions.  The beginning of 2012 also highlighted another chronic problem of the South African mining industry – unstable and insufficient energy supply. 

###### - **Safety-related mining stoppages** 

In line with the South African government’s focus on zero fatalities in the mining industry, work stoppages ordered by the Department of Mineral Resources (DMR) under the decree known as Section 54, became widespread across the PGM mining sector in 2011.  According to Section 54 of the Mine Health and Safety Amendment Act 2008, following any mining fatality, it is now compulsory to shut down the whole mine where the accident took place in order to enable investigation into the cause of this incident.  In addition, these regulations are now being increasingly used by officials as a preventive mechanism for shutting down shafts on suspicion of being unsafe even before an accident occurs, whereas, in the past, only potentially troublesome working areas were shut down for a safety correction to take place in that specific area, allowing the rest of the mine to continue to operate. 

Of course, the increased issuance of Section 54 notices was not unreasonable in the face of a safety performance at PGM mines that deteriorated significantly in 2011.  For example, Amplats, Northam and Lonmin all saw an approximately 50% year-on-year increase in the number of fatalities at their op

erations in their 2011 financial years, while Impala recorded no improvement (seven fatalities in each of 2011 and 2010).  Therefore, it is of little surprise that such stoppages increased dramatically in frequency, particularly after the DMR had opened a new Inspectorate office to cover platinum mines in the PGM-rich Rustenburg area in the second half of 2011.  Amplats reported 81 safety stoppages in calendar 2011 compared with 36 in 2010. And the number of stoppages at its operations in 2011 Q4 was almost as high as in the whole of the previous year. 

The disruption from stoppages is nonetheless having a significant impact on production levels.  Amplats reported a loss of over 161 koz or approximately 5% of the company’s potential platinum production as a result of safety stoppages in 2011.  Other miners including Impala, Lonmin and Aquarius also pointed to the greatly increased frequency of safety stoppages in their financial results as a contributory factor in rising costs and lower-than-planned mine output.  According to the estimations of Cynthia Carroll, the CEO of Anglo, a large number of safety stoppages cost the South African platinum industry more than 300 koz of output in 2011. 

Taking into account the government’s nine-year-old commitment to reduce the number of

###### - **Strikes and industrial action** 

2011 was one of the years for bi-annual wage negotiations in the South African PGM mining industry, and so we went into the year with a heightened risk of strike-related supply disruption. As it turned out, there was little industrial action directly related to the wage negotiations last year, but perhaps only because the wage increases granted by mining companies were some way above the level of domestic inflation.  Nevertheless, there were a number of strikes throughout the industry last year over a range of issues from wages to union recognition to safety.  So labour disrup

One would think that since most PGM producers agreed two-year above-inflation deals last year, the most frequent cause of industrial action – wage disputes – would be less of an issue in 2012. With the PGM sector suffering from high costs of production, heated labour issues, frequent safety stoppages, low metal prices and political pressures, players in the industry are forced either to sell unprofitable assets, scale back existing operations, or join their forces to benefit from the economies of scale.  For instance, in October 2011, Lonmin announced plans to sell a controlling stake (50% plus one share) in Limpopo, its underground and open-pit mine, which has been suspended since 2009 because of poor performance.  Meanwhile, Impala Platinum scrapped its plan to boost output at the Marula mine because of continued underperformance. For the same reason, Aquarius recently announced plans to review operations at its Everest property, and the company intends to maintain production at this mine below maximum capacity while this review is carried out. 

Mining major Anglo American is also making similar noises.  In February 2012, the company announced that it is embarking on a review of the shape and size of its platinum business, which has suffered heavy losses because of numerous safety stoppages.  According to the company’s CEO, Cynthia Carroll, the review will look at the “size and shape of the platinum business and how we can fundamentally shift it and return it to the sort of returns we had in 2008”.  While this review is unlikely to include an outright sale of the business, there has been speculation that Amplats may shut or dispose of some of

its marginal mines. 

While some miners are curtailing their expansion plans or scaling back existing operations, others are looking for partnerships to maintain their growth or develop new properties.  African Rainbow Minerals’ chairman, Patrice Motsepe, said the company is positioning itself for acquisitions and is looking for assets close to existing operations.  Chinese-backed Wesizwe, busy with the construction of its Frischgewaagd-Ledig project, has confirmed it is looking for synergies with its neighbours, particularly around infrastructure and beneficiation.  Village Main Reef CEO, Bernard Swanepoel, said its Lesego platinum project “is too big a project for too small a company.  We need bigger guys with bigger wallets to walk next to us.” 

Operational and labour issues are not the only hurdles facing PGM miners in South Africa. Another potential threat to South African PGM production is coming from the country’s governing party, the African National Congress (ANC).  Earlier this year, the ANC leadership said that, while it had agreed not to seek nationalisation of the country’s mining industry, it could see the benefits to the poor of a 50% tax on producers’ profits.  At present, the standard tax on profits from state mines is only 28%.  A move to take half of all profits could drain funds needed to re-invest in ongoing operations, and will likely reduce the prospective rewards of new development projects and could alter the economics needed for sinking a new mine.  The effect of such a large tax hike would be a rise in overall mining costs which in turn would threaten marginal operations and lower longer-term production growth. 

Based on the assumption that mine disruptions caused by Section 54 stoppages and other issues discussed above will continue, we are of the opinion that South African PGM production will struggle to climb from last year’s levels. g nature of the Zimbabwean political and regulatory environment is well known and it is becoming even tougher. 

First, significant raises of various fees for the mining industry have been implemented in the early months of this year. We are therefore conservative on the growth potential of palladium mining there.  Since the Unki mine reached steady state production only in 2011 Q4, there is still potential for Zimbabwe to produce more metal this year than last although output in 2013 and beyond is unlikely to be higher than 2012 levels.

#### 5.  Market balance and prices 

###### Historical balances 

In our view, six elements combine to determine the palladium price.  The first is industrial demand in autocatalysts and other applications.  Although there is some price elasticity here as platinum’s value fluctuates vis-а-vis those of other PGMs, the main drivers of industrial demand are economic activity and environmental legislation.  The second element is the scrap supply which arises from the recycling of old industrial goods.  Again, although people engaged in the secondary industry may choose to hold or release stocks in response to changes in price, this supply is driven mainly by consumption at various points in the past.  Miners aim to fill the gap between gross demand and secondary supply.  However, the lead time to develop additional mine capacity can often be substantial, so it is hard for them to react quickly to market shortages and higher prices.  The fourth element of the market is instead the most price-sensitive, although it is also perhaps the most marginal for palladium.  This is jewellery demand.  As the margin of supply over other consumption narrows, prices rise and jewellery manufacturers get squeezed. Conversely, when supply moves significantly above other demand, jewellery offtake gets a boost from the lower prices that result.  But this bidding of metal to and from the jewellery sector can be balanced or exacerbated by the accumulation or release of the fifth element in the market, investment stocks.  The final element influencing developments is the sale to the West of palladium stocks previously accumulated by the Russian state. 

During the 1990s and until 2002, the palladium market was mostly in considerable fundamental

deficit. But when adjusted for US and, more particularly, Russian stock changes, metal availability was considerably enhanced. During the 1990s and early 2000s, net Russian exports were persistently higher than our estimate of its mine supply, often exceeding output by a very large margin. Russian sales typically involved much larger volumes of metal than were being moved into or out of exchange warehouses, with shipments in excess of mine output peaking in the late 1990s at almost 2.5 Moz/y. Even at these levels, Russian sales did not always plug the gap between mine plus scrap supply and fabrication demand. However, they did lead to a far more closely balanced market in all but a handful of years. In the decade and a half from 2003, the market was in contrast generally in fundamental surplus, with marked excesses in the years beginning 2006. In 2006-09, despite a decline in mine production, total supply moved significantly above fabricators’ requirements as offtake faltered and secondary output increased. Admittedly, average Russian destocking also slowed in the mid-2000s but, rather than ameliorating deficits, these sales now added to the market’s surplus. Investment demand for the metal has also increased following the launch of palladium Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) backed with physical metal. Nonetheless, large residual surpluses through to 2009 kept the palladium price generally depressed. 2010, however, was one of those rare years when we could observe the palladium market behaving as if distortions of a non-fundamental nature such as investment demand and Russian state sales did not exist at all. An enormous surge in investment demand for palladium generated by the launch of two new ETFs in the USA and Europe in the beginning of that year was strong enough to nearly fully absorb the metal released onto the market from the Russian state reserves and metal exchange warehouses. Our analysis suggests that mine and scrap supply will fail to match palladium fabrication demand in any of the next five years, so that other sources will have to be net suppliers on balance.  Furthermore, from a nearly balanced state in 2012, when we expect the deficit to be as small as 4 koz at this level, the market is set to fall deeper into deficit in each of the years after, so that by the end of our forecast the shortfall will

With time passing, the influence of investment demand on the palladium supply-demand balance is only growing. Such moves pushed the palladium market, which has been in a deficit a year earlier, into a substantial surplus.  Although significantly exhausted after last year’s numerous rounds of heavy redemptions, holdings of palladium in ETF vaults are still substantial; as of the end of February they totalled 1.75 Moz or 25% of annual global mine supply.  As such, the threat that the holders of these instruments may start selling it again is still there.  If this massive hoard of metal finds its way back onto the market, it is likely to shift the final balance back to surplus. Such an outcome can become a reality if the Eurozone crisis gets worse. 

As for palladium deliveries from Russia, their influence on the market is gradually waning along with falling exports from Russia to Switzerland.  Last year they totalled approximately 14.7 tonnes or roughly 473 koz.  This is close to the level of exports in 2010 but much lower than in previous years.  Comments made in the media towards the end of 2011 suggested palladium exports from Russia would last for only two more years and will be at a much lower scale: with stocks now almost exhausted, shipments will fall to just 125-145 koz in each of 2012 and 2013 before they come to a complete halt. #### It’s been a rocky road for gold so far this year 

In 2011, gold completed the tenth year of its record bull run.  Having started the year at $1,388.5/oz (London pm fix), gold soared by 36% to a record $1,920/oz in early September. Subsequent to reaching its new high, prices slipped back to end the year at $1,574.5/oz, only 13% above where they started.  However, if measured on the year

-on-year basis, gold’s 28% gain in 2011 was the second highest since the current bull run commenced in 2001.  The highest rate of annual price appreciation was registered in 2006 when the gold price jumped by 36%. 

After falling throughout the latter months of 2011, gold began the New Year on a sound note, rising by 9% from $1,598/oz, its first fix for the year, to $1,744/oz at the end of January. To be fair, it was not just gold that demonstrated positive performance.  Commodities were generally strong across the board thanks to a US dollar weakness that was the counter to a stronger euro which in turn benefited from the first round of the European quantitative easing programme, launched on 21 December under the name of LTRO (Long-Term Refinancing Operations), plus the US Federal Reserve’s hints that interest rates would remain lower for longer than previously thought. 

The rebound in gold continued until the last day of February, with prices climbing as high as $1,790.80/oz and extending the metal’s gain for the year to 11%.  Right at the end of the month, the bullish sentiment turned very sour, however. Penetration of this level, which was the high made last November, could have provoked a strong bullish response by technical and momentum players.  This final sprint, however, never happened. 

Instead, gold bulls fled the market after Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke failed to mention another round of quantitative easing in his testimony to the US Congress.  A reduced likelihood of additional monetary stimulus in the USA was viewed by many players as a negative for gold, as the metal is seen as a safe store of value and benefits when inflationary fears rise. ###### Investor interest is stabilising while central bank buying continues to provide support 

Since the beginning of this year through to the end of February, combined gold ETF holdings climbed from 71.3 Moz to a new record high of almost 73.0 Moz.  Given the price gains over the same period, one might think this increase of 2.2% shows a somewhat subdued level of activity.  However, what is noticeable is that, during the recent sell-off in December, when the gold price dropped by nearly 10%, aggregate ETF positions were cut by only 2% too.  So our reading is that recent ETF activity points to investors remaining confident in gold’s prospects. The slow pace of growth in combined ETF holdings may also be explained by some investors moving their metal from ETF vaults into allocated accounts or even taking physical deliveries. 

Admittedly, combined ETF holdings have been on a downward trend in the first three weeks of March, and have declined by 0.5% from their record peak in February to 72.5 Moz.  AntiQE3 sentiment from the Fed alongside stronger economic data from the USA has dashed shortterm hopes of further liquidity measures.  At the same time, the strong performance of equity markets around the world has begun to attract investor attention, cooling some interest in gold investments.  Nevertheless, net flows of gold into ETF vaults are still positive for the year despite this recent decline.  That said, at current levels of interest, we do not feel that ETF buying alone is strong enough to prompt a move to higher bullion prices.  Fresh stimuli may be needed to drive their holdings back to record levels and help prices to rise higher. 

According to recent data from the IMF, the official sector remained a net buyer of gold in 2011 for the third consecutive year.  During last year, central banks purchased a total of 402 tonnes of gold and thus increased their combined holdings by more than 13% compared with 2010.  Central banks from Bolivia, Mexico, Russia, South Korea, Turkey and Thailand were amongst the heaviest buyers of gold during 2011.  There was no direct indication of gold buying from the People’s Bank of China but we would be surprised if it is not already active in the market.  There were no significant sellers of gold.

###### Investor fatigue clouds gold prospects in the near term but there is still some gunpowder left down the road 

The past seven months have been putting gold bulls to the test.  Since the early-September highs, there have been four wide swings, and gold prices are currently in retreat from their lateFebruary highs.  With the immediate heat taken out of the EU debt crisis following the second bailout for Greece and with LTRO providing liquidity, the need for safe havens has receded, and that has prompted selling in gold.  However, many of the underlying driving forces for higher gold prices from 2011 remain in place.  Extreme economic uncertainty, low real interest rates, high developing world inflation and the prospect of European sovereign debt defaults will accompany us throughout 2012.  As such, although we would not be surprised to see gold prices testing the bottom border of a bullish channel, we generally expect dips to be well supported. 

Even though, in the

near term, the greatest threat to the world economy is deflation as growth slows in Asia and recession looms in Europe, the legacy of all these massive rounds of quantitative easing in both the USA and the EU is likely to be inflationary down the road.  Even once the EU debt crisis is under control, liquidity is likely to remain high as governments will be unwilling to jeopardise early recovery by raising interest rates.  This has the potential to stoke inflationary expectations and launch another leg of gold’s bull run.  The picture in the USA is similar to that in Europe.  In January, US policy makers reiterated their intention to keep the benchmark interest rate unchanged at a record low through to late 2014 and made no changes to the Operation Twist programme to replace shorter-term Treasuries in the Fed’s balance sheet with longer-term debt. 

The situation is rather different in the larger developing economies.  Of particular interest are the major gold consumers, India and China.  Both have struggled with high inflation and are making efforts to control this.  Until better control over inflation is exerted, gold will remain attractive as a wealth hedge in these countries. 

We are, however, concerned that some risk fatigue seems to be developing in the gold market, with greater market stresses needed to drive each fresh wave of buying interest.  Signs

#### 2.  Regional developments 

###### 2.1  The Americas: US recovery maintains momentum 

In the final analysis US GDP growth in the fourth quarter was revised up to 3% quarter-onquarter annualised.  Subsequently growth has eased, as the temporary factors at work at the end of 2011 have subsided.  Nonetheless, high frequency data, relating to employment, retail sales including autos, and manufacturing, reinforce our view that the USA is recovering steadily, and on course to gain a little momentum beyond the first quarter.  This is as we expect, but still at a pace well below that evident in past upturns. 

Non-farm payrolls increased by a net 227,000 in February.  This was the third consecutive month in which employment rose by more than 200,000.  But, due to an increase in the participation rate, the unemployment rate stayed at 8.3%, versus 9.1% six months ago. 

Consumer confidence has improved as a result of the firming labour market, and this is translating into stronger consumer spending.  Thus retail sales expanded by 1.1% month-onmonth in February.  This was their fastest growth in five months, and it lifted them 6.5% yearon-year.  The pick-up was led by autos which rose 6.4%, following a 4.7% month-on-month rise in January.  The steady rise in retail sales has helped keep the inventory to sales ratio steady at 1.27 months for the past half year. 

The underlying advance in retail sales, allied with stock replenishment, and helped at the margin by exports, continues to support output.  Although industrial production stagnated in February manufacturing output increased by 0.4% month-on-month.  In fact it was held back by a contraction in auto assembly, which was to an extent a payback after the strong 8.6% monthon-month gain in January.  Recent survey data point to further output growth in the near term. Encouragingly the volume of unfilled manufacturing orders rose 0.6% month-on-month in January. 

What this amounts to is evidence that the recovery is sustained, and gaining in traction. However, as we have argued before, it is very modest given the depth of the downturn in 2009, and compared with the pace of earlier upswings. 

This is evident first and foremost in the labour market.  In addition to its inflation mandate the Federal Reserve (Fe

d) is tasked with maintaining the economy at full employment, which equates to an unemployment rate around 5%.  However, we are unlikely to see an acceleration sufficient to transform the labour market to this extent any time soon.  A recent survey showed that a majority of employers remain reluctant to hire in the short term.  Thus the labour market continues to mend slowly, and will struggle to up this performance as federal layoffs gather pace in 2013.  Put another way, output growth would have to pick up to something like 4% per year for a sustained period to bring the unemployment rate towards the full employment target swiftly, implying net job creation in the 300,000-400,000 per month range.  As things stand full employment is unlikely to be reached until the end of the decade. 

The factors holding firms back from ramping up their recruitment appear to be similarly holding back investment.  This is why we have business investment expanding 2-3 percentage points more slowly in this recovery than for example in the upturn after the recession in the early 1990s.

###### 2.2  Europe: Eurozone far from safe 

European authorities have made some progress in stemming the crisis that threatened to engulf the region towards the end of 2011.  In particular, the ECB’s recent interventions have significantly calmed financial markets, and helped avert a potentially catastrophic credit crunch. Furthermore, Greece has managed to secure a new round of bailout funding and has negotiated a debt swap aimed at reducing its debt burden, albeit at the expense of even deeper spending cu

ts, and closer monitoring of its finances.  However, we remain sceptical that this will be enough to solve Greece’s fiscal mess in the long run.  Also, the let-up in bank funding pressures since December has not translated into lending to the real economy, which is showing signs of further deterioration as 2012 progresses.  Broadly positive developments since last month have also been countered by the effects of rising oil prices, which now threaten to constrain any recovery in the consumer sector by reducing real incomes, and in the corporate sector by hitting businesses, which are already suffering from weak demand at home and abroad, with higher input costs. 

Eurozone financial markets have improved in recent weeks, aided by a further injection of liquidity from the ECB in late February.  The 3-year lending operation – LTRO – saw around 800 banks borrow €530 billion, resulting in a net liquidity injection of around €300 billion.  In the space of two months, the ECB has now injected over €1 trillion into the financial system, banishing the threat of a credit crunch, which was a major worry in late 2011.  The fact that 800 banks used the latest LTRO – compared with 492 in December – suggests that a greater number of smaller banks gained access to funding, helped by the ECB's decision to expand the range of eligible collateral.  Banks in the peripheral countries have been the heaviest users of the LTRO, being the ones that faced the hardest liquidity squeeze in interbank markets.  Spanish and Italian banks are now financing around 5% of their assets from the ECB, and some of the LTRO funds have been recycled into increased purchases of government debt, helping bring down yields from the dangerous levels seen late last year. 

Financial markets have also been buoyed up by the agreement of a €130 billion second bailout package for Greece, and a debt swap process. ###### 2.3  Asia: despite fears to contrary, China on track 

As we approach the end of the first quarter and peer through the statistical fog, it looks as though the Chinese economy is shaping up broadly as we had expected: inflation is slowing, activity is decelerating further – though not collapsing – and policy is being loosened, albeit less quickly than we had anticipated.  We will have a clearer picture next month when GDP figures for the period are released.  To date there has been little evidence that the economy will imminently regain momentum and we continue to expect that a pick-up in activity will be weighted towards the second half of the year.  And when recovery does arrive it is likely to be subdued by past standards as we expect policy makers to take a more gradualist approach to stimulating the economy than has been the case in the past.  Our forecast for GDP growth remains at 8.3% this year, although this is conditional on the absence of significant external shocks – notably from a sovereign debt driven implosion of the Eurozone – which we see as the key downside risk. 

With the economy slowing, already skittish sentiment has been unsettled by the government’s 2012 growth target of 7.5%, announced at this month’s National People’s Congress (NPC).  However, in our view there is little new in the announcement.  For one thing, the five year plan that was unveiled last year had a 7% annual growth target at its centre.  For another, in only one year in the past two decades has the growth target not been exceeded.  In other words the target should be seen as a floor for this year’s growth. 

The slowdown in China is largely a response to the domestic policy tightening that was implemented to rein in an over exuberant real estate sector and escalating inflation, although clearly the weakness of overseas markets has also contributed to the deceleration in activity by limiting export growth.  In the first two months, heavy industry drove a drop in industrial production growth to 11.4% year-on-year, a 2½-year low.  Official figures that strip out the seasonal fluctuations in output show that three-month on three-month growth fell to 8.8% annualised in February from 10.1% in the prior three months.  These figures have a short history and as such are relatively untested, but they accord with anecdotal evidence that the economy continued to lose momentum in the early part of this year. #### 3.  Alternative scenarios: oil shock 

The benchmark Brent oil price has risen sharply through the first quarter, from an average around $110/bbl in the final quarter of 2011 to a recent spot record of $127/bbl, and a range around $125/bbl.  In euro terms it is at all-time highs already. 

This been driven partly by non-Opec supply difficulties and partly by rising political tensions in the Gulf.  When prices were last at this level in the first half of 2011, in the wake of the Arab Spring, they contributed to the deceleration of economic growth in the second half of the year. Thus there is reason to think that a renewed burst of energy price inflation may stunt growth. 

Although Saudi Arabia is taking steps to defuse the market, which it appears to equate with returning the price to around $100/bbl, further supply disruptions could easily cause the risk premium to rise further and drive prices up to $150/bbl.  More ominously, an outbreak of hostilities, for example between Iran and Israel and the USA, could readily cause prices to surge to $200/bbl.  In both cases the real economy would pay a price.  Our alternative scenarios examine the impact of oil rising to $150/bbl and to $200/bbl, although beyond the shock we allow the price of oil to revert towards a more fundamentally determined value, as the consequences of demand destruction emerge. 

As Table A2 shows, the effect of another $25/bbl increase in the price of Brent would be relatively moderate.  Our simulation suggests that growth would decelerate by 10-20 bp in 2012, and by 40-50 bp in 2013, although we have made no assumptions about collateral damage to confidence, and the effect that might have on savings rates and financial markets.  As prices begin to revert to their trend path from 2014, however, growth would get a moderate 10-20 bp fillip. 

If prices rose to $200/bbl, however, the consequences would be much more severe.  Growth in 2013 in particular would be almost 1 percentage point lower than in our base case. #### More exchange rate volatility 

In our forecasts short to medium-term parities are influenced by market-making factors, such as comparative interest rates, which are of a cyclical nature, and inflation expectations, trade deficits and relative growth rates, which are of a more structural nature.  Increasingly, however, some of these structural influences may act in opposition to cyclical influences.  For instance, a currency may not weaken much in response to cuts in interest rates that are made mainly to support growth.  In the long term, however, currencies are projected to revert towards their `fair’ values, which are closely akin to the values implied by purchasing power parities.  In other words currencies are forecast to revert to cross-parities that compensate for the varying prices, in local currency terms, of a common basket of goods.
